This represents his first known cardiac event. He reports being physically active at baseline and denies cigarette smoking. He reports whiskey consumption approximately three to four times weekly. He reports no regular medications. The need for emergent coronary angiography and possible PCI was discussed directly with him.

Neurologic: Alert and appropriately interactive without gross focal neurologic deficit.

Extremities: No gross cyanosis.
Laboratory data reviewed. ECG demonstrates findings consistent with an acute inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction.

2.Chest and epigastric discomfort secondary to acute coronary syndrome (ICD-10: R07.9)
3.Obesity (ICD-10: E66.9)

Plan •High-complexity medical decision-making performed due to an acute STEMI representing an immediate threat to life and cardiac function and requiring emergent invasive coronary evaluation with potential revascularization.
•Continue STEMI protocol and proceed immediately to the cardiac catheterization laboratory.
•Perform urgent coronary angiography to define coronary anatomy and identify the culprit lesion.
•If an appropriate culprit obstruction is identified, proceed with percutaneous coronary intervention as clinically indicated, potentially including aspiration/thrombectomy, balloon angioplasty, and coronary stent placement.
•If angiography demonstrates extensive or anatomically unfavorable multivessel or left-main coronary disease, consider urgent cardiothoracic surgical evaluation for CABG rather than PCI.
•Acute STEMI antiplatelet/antithrombotic therapy and subsequent secondary-prevention therapy to be guided by angiographic findings, hemodynamics, laboratory results, and clinical course.
•Continuous telemetry and close hemodynamic monitoring.
•Serially review CBC, renal function, electrolytes, cardiac biomarkers, lipid profile, and HbA1c as appropriate.
•Obtain echocardiographic assessment of LV systolic function and regional wall motion after stabilization.
•Further recommendations following coronary angiography.

Informed Consent / Procedural Discussion
The suspected acute myocardial infarction and need for emergent coronary angiography with possible PCI were discussed directly with the patient. Coronary angiography will define the location and severity of coronary obstruction. If a treatable culprit lesion is identified, intervention may proceed immediately, potentially including aspiration/thrombectomy, balloon angioplasty, and coronary stent placement.
The possibility of severe or multiple coronary blockages requiring consideration of coronary artery bypass surgery rather than PCI was also discussed. Risks, benefits, alternatives, and the emergent nature of the procedure were reviewed, including bleeding, vascular injury, contrast-related renal injury or reaction, arrhythmia, stroke, myocardial infarction, emergency surgery, and death. The patient expressed understanding and agreed to proceed.
Nursing Communication •Continue STEMI protocol, telemetry, and close hemodynamic monitoring.
•Maintain readiness for immediate transfer to the cardiac catheterization laboratory.
•Notify the treating cardiology team immediately for recurrent/worsening chest discomfort, significant arrhythmia, hypotension, or other clinical deterioration.
•Activity per acute STEMI protocol pending catheterization and stabilization.

 3.  Questionable pyelonephritis versus gastrointestinal source?  Colitis
–Patient presented acute onset periumbilical abdominal pain and associated nausea vomiting.  Per daughter, patient deals with intermittent constipation and diarrhea at home.  On presentation patient Tmax was 37.9, heart rate in the 90s, maintaining maps in 65, respiratory rate 24, saturating well room air.  Lab work without leukocytosis, creatinine of 0.8, procalcitonin of 18.4 which improved to 10.5, blood culture growing Klebsiella aerogenes pansensitive.  UA with negative leukocyte esterase and nitrites and urine culture with no growth.  CT abdomen pelvis showed some apparent wall thickening in the descending colon/distal transverse colon  without any distention, there was hypoattenuation in the right renal interpolar region with question of striated nephrogram concerning for possible pyelonephritis, and scattered colonic diverticula.  Patient is repeat blood culture 9/1 are negative.  Patient was empirically treated with ceftriaxone transition Cipro and Flagyl.  No definitive source of infection was not identified.  Although I suppose pyelonephritis is still possible, less likely given negative UA.  Although Klebsiella aerogenes is not a typical bug associated with colon cancer, it is found in GI system and given changes of some transverse colon thickening she can consider outpatient colonoscopy if has recurrent bacteremia or no recent colonoscopy.  I advised patient to discuss risks and benefits with primary care provider.  I did discharge she was clinically doing well, no fevers, denied any further episodes of nausea or vomiting, no UTI symptoms, abdomen was soft and nontender.  Patient did have some diarrhea, on the morning of discharge reported small amounts, loose/watery which was attributed to bowel regimen.  Patient was discharged home with Cipro and Flagyl for 5 more days to complete a 7-day treatment from negative blood culture.

- Never invent or infer names, MRNs, FINs, DOBs, phones, rooms, locations, dates, diagnoses, medications, labs, vitals, imaging, EF, wall motion, anatomy, device data, procedure results, or time.
- CPT rule: Never create a CPT for a procedure that was not performed or documented. When a procedure is explicitly documented and no CPT was given in the trigger, identify and include the standard CPT code(s) for that documented procedure from coding knowledge. If the physician explicitly dictates or requests a CPT code, use that exact code — do not substitute, upgrade, downgrade, or infer a different E/M level. A physician-dictated CPT overrides any CPT that would otherwise be inferred from encounter type words such as "consult," "progress note," or "follow-up." Example: if the physician says "Generate 99233," the note and SLIM must say 99233, not 99223.
- ICD-10 rule: Never create a diagnosis that was not documented. For every diagnosis explicitly stated or clearly established in the physician's dictation or source material, automatically identify and include the corresponding ICD-10-CM code — the physician is not required to dictate ICD-10 numbers. When a diagnosis is too nonspecific to determine a reliable code, use the most accurate supported code or briefly flag the ambiguity.
- DOS rule: The SLIM Billing Block must always include the Date of Service determined from the physician's dictation or the encounter being documented. Do not substitute the date the note is generated if the service occurred on a different date.
- Binary program-status and demographic fields (RPM enrollment, CCM enrollment, language, interpreter status, and similar) must never be filled with a definitive value — positive or negative — when no explicit source statement exists. Absence of information is not a negative finding. Use `Not Provided` when the field is not mentioned in the dictation or source material.

Do not use `[Not Provided]` for CPT or ICD-10 when the procedure or diagnosis is clearly documented — derive the code. `[Not Provided]` for CPT or ICD-10 is reserved only for information that genuinely cannot be determined from the clinical documentation or standard coding knowledge.

- Every Cerner output (progress note, consult, critical care, procedure report, pre-procedure H&P, cardiac catheterization report) must end with its own SLIM Billing Block. ### 10.4 Standalone short summary

Trigger: user requests a "short summary" or "summary for [patient]" during an active Rhythm Monitoring session.

This is a valid generation trigger and bypasses the HARD HOLD GATE. It does not produce the 3-bullet report (10.1) or folder output (10.2). It does not end or restart the session — after outputting, return to HOLD.

Output format: 2–3 concise sentences, no bullets, no heading.

Every short summary must begin with:

```
[INITIALS] - [Full Patient Name]: [summary text]
```

Rules:
- Preserve the physician's exact wording. Do not substitute, simplify, or reinterpret qualified statements.
- Do not add interpretation, clinical correlation, or conclusions beyond what was dictated.
- Do not include any treatment recommendation, medication name, or clinical action unless the physician dictated that exact phrase.
- No CPT code, date, study duration, or formatting beyond the identifier line and sentences.

Example:
```
JER VAL - Jeremy Valdez: Predominant sinus rhythm with rare ectopic beats. SVT is possible, but visible P waves favor sinus tachycardia.
```
